stories.headline: Senate Republicans break through Washington gridlock with massive American energy, data center overhaul
stories.note: Senate Republicans pushed a sweeping permitting and energy overhaul past gridlock with a big bipartisan vote, a lame-duck win on building and energy.
body: Senate Republicans moved a major permitting overhaul forward Thursday night, advancing the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 with a large bipartisan vote after months of stops and starts and late input from the White House.

The package is designed to speed up environmental reviews, narrow the window for lawsuits against projects, protect projects once they are approved, expand the power grid, and make it easier to develop every kind of energy, from oil and gas to renewables.

It also takes on data centers, a hot issue with voters. Data centers drawing at least 20 megawatts would have to cover the cost of the extra power they need, post financial guarantees for new or upgraded facilities, and pay for leftover infrastructure costs if they pull out of an area. Democrat Martin Heinrich, the bill's lead Democrat, pushed for that ratepayer language.
Sen. Shelley Moore Capito, who chairs the Environment and Public Works Committee, has pitched the bill as a way to build infrastructure faster without giving up environmental protections.

The House is the next hurdle. Sen. Alan Armstrong of Oklahoma, who has made permitting reform his top issue, said much of the text came from House work and that there's support on both sides, though he worried about lawmakers actually showing up for the vote.
Why it matters: With Democrats about to take both chambers, Republicans are using the lame duck to lock in a long-sought goal of cutting red tape for American energy and construction.

stories.headline: Trump scores key win over House progressive accused of assaulting ICE agent
stories.note: A federal appeals court refused to rehear Rep. LaMonica McIver's immunity claim, keeping assault charges from the Delaney Hall ICE clash alive.
body: The Trump administration won another round in court Thursday against Rep. LaMonica McIver, D-N.J., who is charged in connection with a May 2025 confrontation with ICE agents at the Delaney Hall detention center in Newark.

The 3rd Circuit Court of Appeals denied McIver's request to reconsider its August 2026 ruling, which held that the Constitution's Speech or Debate Clause doesn't shield her from at least two of the three charges. The third count was sent back to a lower court.

Prosecutors allege McIver drove her forearm into an officer trying to arrest Newark Mayor Ras Baraka and later struck an officer with both forearms while going back into the secured area. The panel majority, a Biden appointee and a Trump appointee, called pushing past and striking someone "unambiguously non-legislative."

McIver blamed a "weaponized" Justice Department, said she faces 17 years in prison for doing oversight of ICE, and said her lawyers are weighing every option. Dissenting Judge Thomas Ambro argued that blocking a member from a DHS facility undermines oversight. The case could end up at the Supreme Court.

Why it matters: The ruling undercuts Democrats' argument that a member of Congress can claim legislative immunity for a physical clash with federal agents, a win for the administration's defense of ICE officers.

stories.headline: Trump ally Bill Essayli tapped to lead investigation of Biden officials over Mar-a-Lago raid
stories.note: The DOJ tapped Trump ally Bill Essayli to probe whether Biden officials broke the law in the 2022 Mar-a-Lago raid, keeping the 'grand conspiracy' investigation moving.
body: Bill Essayli, the first assistant U.S. attorney in Los Angeles, will serve as a special assistant investigating whether Biden Justice Department officials broke federal law when they carried out the 2022 search warrant at President Trump's Mar-a-Lago estate, two sources told Fox News Digital.

The Mar-a-Lago search kicked off Jack Smith's classified documents case. Essayli's work is part of a broader "grand conspiracy" probe that then-Attorney General Pam Bondi opened in August 2025 to look at Obama-era officials, which has since widened to whether Biden officials conspired to unlawfully prosecute Trump.

He is the latest prosecutor on the case after two departures: Joe diGenova resigned in September amid frustration over the lack of charges, and Jason Reding Quiñones, the U.S. attorney for South Florida, resigned abruptly a few weeks ago. Essayli will split time between Florida and Los Angeles.

There is controversy. A federal judge ruled in October that Essayli was unlawfully serving as a "de facto" U.S. attorney in Los Angeles and disqualified him from supervising two prosecutions; the DOJ is appealing. House Democrats led by Rep. Dave Min have demanded an ethics probe, and a defense attorney who challenged him accused the administration of installing "minions."
Why it matters: The administration is signaling it intends to keep pressing for accountability over the Mar-a-Lago raid, with a loyal, aggressive prosecutor now in charge.

stories.headline: Dems, GOP rebels fail to rein in Trump's Iran war in Senate, but bigger battle looms
stories.note: Senate Democrats and a few GOP rebels failed again to pass a war powers rebuke of Trump's Iran campaign, and even some Democrats admit they're in a tough spot on defense funding.
body: Senate Democrats couldn't win over enough Republicans to pass a non-binding resolution rebuking President Trump's war against Iran, their first try since the midterms. GOP Sens. Susan Collins, Lisa Murkowski and Rand Paul sided with them, but it wasn't enough.

The measure, which passed the House in September under Rep. Seth Moulton, would have called for pulling troops from hostilities Congress hadn't authorized. Because it was non-binding, it would not have gone to Trump's desk even if it passed.

Democrats are now eyeing the Dec. 11 government funding deadline as leverage. Majority Leader John Thune warned Democrats may try to force a third shutdown this year, which he called a terrible outcome. Sen. Tim Kaine countered that Democrats won't shut the government down and that Republicans would own any standoff.

After a long closed-door meeting with Deputy Defense Secretary Steve Feinberg, Republicans set aside, for now, a plan to move a $350 billion war request through reconciliation and decided to give Democrats a chance on regular appropriations. Sen. Chris Coons admitted Democrats are "in a really tough place" balancing opposition to the war with support for the troops.
Why it matters: Democrats' latest push to tie Trump's hands fell short, and their own divisions over funding the military give Republicans an opening heading into the December deadline.

stories.headline: Van Hollen scores support from another Dem amid Senate majority leader bid
stories.note: Sen. Elissa Slotkin joined the push to dump Chuck Schumer for Chris Van Hollen, widening Democrats' leadership civil war.
body: Sen. Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., said Thursday she will back Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., who launched a challenge last week to unseat Chuck Schumer as the Democrats' Senate leader.

In a video, Slotkin said she doesn't think Schumer is best positioned to lead and that, since she wasn't supporting him, she would back Van Hollen. She added that whoever wins must show how they will bring in the next generation and lay out bold ideas for the first 100 days.

Van Hollen shared her post, saying the two agree the country needs "new leadership" in the Senate. Incoming Michigan Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed and Minnesota Sen.-elect Peggy Flanagan, both Van Hollen backers, amplified it too, with El-Sayed adding a raised-fist emoji.
Democrats won both chambers in the 2026 midterms and will hold the majorities when the 120th Congress opens early next year.
Why it matters: Before they even take power, Senate Democrats are openly feuding over who leads them, with the party's left flank lining up against Schumer.

stories.headline: EXCLUSIVE: Retired police sergeant issues warning over Mamdani's NYPD shake-up ahead of Thanksgiving parade
stories.note: A veteran police sergeant warns Mamdani's move to disband the NYPD's elite Strategic Response Group is dangerous ahead of the Thanksgiving parade, while far-left groups cheer it.
body: Retired Sgt. Betsy Brantner Smith, a National Police Association spokesperson with 29 years in Chicago-area policing, told Fox News Digital she wouldn't bring her own family to New York right now, after Mayor Zohran Mamdani moved to disband the NYPD's Strategic Response Group.

The roughly 500-officer unit handles counterterrorism support, major-event security and protest response. Smith said its officers train and work together and know how to handle fast-moving threats, including active shooters, and she worried intelligence could be lost before big events like the 100th Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade on Nov. 26.

Mamdani says counterterrorism and protest response are different jobs and that police will always show up for violence. His overhaul bans long guns and tear gas at protests, limits pepper spray, and creates a new First Amendment Support Team and Patrol Support Division, plus a civilian-led de-escalation office in 2028. The NYPD says parade security is unaffected because the new units don't start until February 2027, and Commissioner Jessica Tisch defended the plan.

Smith called it "a political decision" and "an incredibly dangerous one." Far-left groups including the Party for Socialism and Liberation, Within Our Lifetime and streamer Hasan Piker praised the move, while the National Police Association's petition to restore the unit drew nearly 2,000 signatures in two days.

Why it matters: New York's socialist mayor is reshaping the nation's largest police force in ways cheered by activists and criticized by law enforcement, a ready-made public safety contrast for Republicans.
